newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIUM'S SCANDAL-HIT SOCIALISTS LOSE LEAD IN POLL.
newsitem.headline: BELGIUM'S SCANDAL-HIT SOCIALISTS LOSE LEAD IN POLL.

text.p: Belgium's scandal-hit francophone Socialist Party (PS) has been ousted by the PRL liberals as the leading party in Belgium's southern region of Wallonia, according to a newspaper poll published on Monday.

The quarterly poll of voting intentions in La Libre Belgique showed support for the PS in Wallonia slipping to 27.3 percent from 30.5 percent in December and compared to 33.8 percent at the May 1995 general election.

Confidence in the PS has been shaken by allegations it received bribes from Italian helicopter firm Agusta and French avionics company Dassault in the late 1980's in return for contracts. Both companies have repeatedly denied wrongdoing.

In recent weeks the party has been further weakened by the arrest of three senior officials under investigation in the Dassault affair, and the resignation of a former party chairman from the presidency of the Walloon regional assembly.
La Libre said that in addition a growing number of socialist sympathisers were becoming disenchanted with PS policies.
Support for the PRL rose to 29.6 percent from 28.8 percent in December and 24.0 percent in May 1995, depriving the PS of the top spot in the poll for the first time in ten years.

In the Dutch-speaking northern region of Flanders, Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene's Christian democrat CVP party increased its lead over the Flemish VLD liberals, with 27.2 percent of the share compared to 25.8 percent three months ago.
Together, the French and Dutch speaking christian democrat and the socialist parties form Belgium's four-party federal government.

A majority of those polled - 58 percent - said they did not have confidence in the Federal government, down slightly from 60 percent at the previous poll. An unchanged 19 percent did have confidence in the government, and the rest had no opinion.
The poll was carried out between March 9 and 12 by Marketing Unit on 2,000 Belgians across the country aged 18 and over. It had an error margin of 2.25 percent, the paper said.
The next general election in Belgium is due to take place by the end of 1999, although many observers expect it to be called some time next year.
